case_name: Satyaendra Dayal Khare v State of Maharashtra
respondent:
State of Maharashtra
Supreme Court of India

2 August 2005
Cr.A. No. 953 of 2005 (Arising out of S.L.P. (Cri.) No. 3304 of 2004)
The Order of the Court was as follows:
Leave granted.
1.  We have heard learned Senior Counsel for the appellant and the counsel for the State. The appellant, during the relevant time, was the Collector of Customs working at Sahar Airport, Mumbai. He was prosecuted for the offences punishable under Sections 341, 342 and 354 of the Penal Code.
2. The trial court acquitted the appellant of the charges framed against him and aggrieved by the same, the State of Maharashtra preferred an appeal before the High Court and the appellate court reversed the finding of the trial court and found him guilty of offence punishable under Section 354 IPC and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of six months and to pay a fine of Rs 25,000, in default, to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of one month. However, the acquit
facts: The case against the appellant was initiated on the basis of information furnished by PW 1, the complainant, who was a member of the Indian Revenue Services and who was undergoing training as a Probationary Officer.

The complainant alleged that the accused led her to his chamber and switched on a VCR and displayed a film relating to seizure of some contraband gold and when this film was being viewed, the complainant was seated on a sofa and the appellant was standing behind and thereafter the appellant caught hold of her hand and pushed her down in the sofa.

The complainant came out of the room and she wanted to get back to her hostel and when she came to the exit point and desired to have a taxi and at that time the official car was already there at that place and the appellant pushed her inside the car and thereafter she was taken in the car and because of her insistence she was dropped at the railway station.

The complainant reached her room in the hostel and contacted PW 7, a co-trainee, who was staying in the same hostel and at 9.30 in the night she telephonically contacted PW 10, the Director General of National Academy of Customs, Excise and Narcotics and gave the details of the entire incident that had happened in the office of the appellant.
The complainant also had given information to her husband who was working at Hyderabad.
issues: Whether the view taken by the Magistrate was reasonable and the witnesses were rightly disbelieved
Whether the prosecution suppressed the evidence and material witnesses
Whether the High Court rightly reversed the finding entered by the learned Magistrate
petitioner_arguments: The view taken by the Magistrate was reasonable and the witnesses were rightly disbelieved
The prosecution suppressed the evidence and material witnesses
There was delay in lodging the complaint before the police
There was evidence to the effect that the complainant was deliberately making a concocted story to foist a false case against the appellant
respondent_arguments: The reasons given by the Magistrate were not sustainable
The High Court rightly reversed the same
The complainant, being a trainee officer, would naturally look forward to get some help from her superior officer, PW 10, and she gave a detailed narration of the incident that had happened
court_reasoning: We find no reasons for her to file a false complaint against the appellant
The complainant, being a trainee officer, would naturally look forward to get some help from her superior officer, PW 10, and she gave a detailed narration of the incident that had happened
Some minor contradictions have been brought out, and they are not of serious nature

In her complaint she has stated that she vomited while she was in the chamber of the appellant. At the time of giving evidence she stated that saliva had come out of her mouth, and it is pointed out by appellant's counsel that there was no evidence to prove that the presence of any remnants of food particles or material in the room of the appellant to prove that she had vomited
The acts committed by the appellant would certainly come within the purview of the offence punishable under Section 354
holding: The appellant is on bail and his bail bonds are discharged.
